extracted.intended_audience: K–12 mathematics educators, curriculum designers, assessment developers, and professional development providers (California)
extracted.subtask_description: K–12 Common Core Standards describing eight mathematical practices that students should develop; intended to guide instruction, curriculum, assessment, and professional development in mathematics. Emphasizes processes/proficiencies and connections between practice and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals; make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution; and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, try special cases and simpler forms, monitor and evaluate their progress, and change course if necessary. Students draw diagrams, graph data, search for regularity, and can explain correspondences between representations. Younger students may use concrete objects or pictures; older students might transform algebraic expressions or change graphing windows. Students check answers using a different method and continually ask, 'Does this make sense?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage planning before computation, use special cases and simpler forms to gain insight, teach monitoring strategies (self-checks, alternate methods). Discourage immediate, unplanned computation ('jumping in'). Use cross-representation checks (equation↔graph↔table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason abstractly and quantitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Students make sense of quantities and their relationships. They decontextualize—abstract a situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate symbols independently—and contextualize—pause to probe the referents of symbols. Quantitative reasoning includes creating coherent representations, considering units, attending to the meaning of quantities (not just computations), and flexibly using properties of operations and objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach both abstraction (symbolic modeling) and re-linking to context (interpretation of results and units). Emphasize unit analysis, dimensional thinking, and flexible use of properties rather than rote manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and established results to construct arguments. They make conjectures, build logical progressions to test conjectures, break situations into cases, and recognize/use counterexamples. They justify conclusions, communicate them, and respond to others' arguments. They reason inductively about data and compare effectiveness of plausible arguments, distinguishing correct logic from flawed reasoning. Elementary students use concrete referents (objects, drawings) for arguments; later students determine domains of applicability. The page also notes that students build proofs by induction and proofs by contradiction (CA 3.1) for higher mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach use of definitions and previously established results; provide opportunities to produce and critique arguments. Use counterexamples to test claims. Scaffold from concrete arguments to formal proofs; introduce induction and contradiction where appropriate. Emphasize clear justification and the ability to explain flaws in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model with mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Students apply mathematics to solve problems from everyday life, society, and the workplace. Early grades: write simple equations to describe situations. Middle grades: use proportional reasoning to plan events or analyze community problems. High school: use geometry or functions to model design problems or relationships. Proficient modelers make assumptions and approximations to simplify situations (with readiness to revise), identify important quantities and map relationships with diagrams, tables, graphs, flowcharts, and formulas, analyze relationships mathematically, interpret results in context, and improve models when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include real-world tasks that require making assumptions, choosing variables, and interpreting results. Teach iterative model-building: simplify, analyze, interpret, validate, and revise. Emphasize translating between real situation and mathematical representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate tools strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Students consider available tools—pencil and paper, concrete models, rulers, protractors, calculators, spreadsheets, computer algebra systems, statistical packages, dynamic geometry software—and decide when each is helpful, recognizing insights and limitations. Proficient students detect possible errors via estimation and other knowledge. Technology can visualize effects of changing assumptions and compare predictions with data. Students identify and use relevant external mathematical resources (including digital content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster familiarity with a range of tools so students can choose strategically. Teach estimating and error-detection strategies. Provide tasks where technology provides insight (visualization, data analysis) while also discussing its limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Students strive to communicate precisely: using clear definitions, stating the meaning of chosen symbols (including consistent use of the equal sign), specifying units of measure, and labeling axes. They calculate accurately and express numerical answers with appropriate precision for context. Elementary students give carefully formulated explanations; by high school students examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model precise language and notation, insist on units and labeled representations, teach appropriate significant figures and context-dependent precision. Address common imprecision anti-patterns (ambiguous symbols, unlabeled axes, inconsistent equals usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for and make use of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Students discern patterns or structure in mathematics. Examples: noticing commutativity (3+7 = 7+3), recognizing distributive decompositions (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3), factoring (x^2 + 9x + 14 seen as 2×7 and 2 + 7), recognizing significant lines in geometry and drawing auxiliary lines. Students step back for an overview and shift perspective, seeing complicated expressions as single objects or as composed of objects (e.g., 5 − 3(x − y)^2 as 5 minus a nonnegative term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that highlight algebraic and geometric structure and techniques for exploiting them (factoring, decomposition, auxiliary constructions). Teach perspective shifts (whole ↔ parts) as an explicit strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Students notice repeated calculations and seek general methods or shortcuts. Examples: recognizing a repeating decimal from repeated division steps; abstracting a slope formula from repeated slope checks; noticing cancellation patterns that lead to general formulas (e.g., sum of a geometric series). While solving, students maintain oversight of the process and continually evaluate reasonableness of intermediate results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage pattern spotting in computations and deriving general procedures from repetition. Use examples where students perform repeated steps and are prompted to generalize. Teach meta-cognitive oversight (monitor intermediate results) alongside procedural generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying processes and proficiencies (NCTM and NRC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practices rest on two sets of long-standing processes/proficiencies: the NCTM process standards—problem solving, reasoning and proof, communication, representation, and connections—and the NRC Adding It Up strands—adaptive reasoning, strategic competence, conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, and productive disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these named processes and proficiencies as lenses when implementing the practices: design instruction and assessment that develops strategic competence, conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, adaptive reasoning, productive disposition, and the NCTM processes. Treat them as foundational learning goals that inform tasks and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect the Standards for Mathematical Practice to the Standards for Mathematical Content
rubrics_metrics.description: The practices describe how student practitioners should engage with mathematics across grades. Designers of curricula, assessments, and professional development should connect mathematical practices to mathematical content. Content standards that use the word 'understand' are especially good opportunities to connect practices to content because lack of understanding prevents engagement in the practices. Points of intersection should be weighted toward central, generative concepts that merit investment of time and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing curriculum or assessment, identify content standards that expect understanding and explicitly map which practices students should use with that content. Prioritize central/generative topics for deeper practice integration, and use these intersections to guide instruction, assessment, and PD focus.
